content: International reference materials for ferritin have been developed to calibrate working standards used in routine laboratory assays and to evaluate and standardize new tests for ferritin quantification. The WHO international standard for ferritin, provided by the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control (NIBSC, code 94/572), is commercially available and recommended for use in all assays. It is critical that reference materials are both commutable and traceable to the WHO reference standard to ensure consistency of results across different procedures and to prevent calibration bias. Quality controls should be included in every assay run, or at least daily, on instruments measuring ferritin. Ideally, these quality controls should cover low, medium, and high ferritin concentrations. Laboratories conducting ferritin measurements for patient care or public health assessments should participate in external quality assurance programs. In regions with widespread infection or inflammation, serum ferritin should be measured alongside acute-phase response proteins, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP), to account for inflammation-related increases in ferritin levels. Adjustments for inflammation can be made by raising the ferritin cut-off values (e.g., to 30 µg/L or 70 µg/L depending on the age group), excluding individuals with elevated CRP or AGP levels, or using regression correction methods to adjust ferritin concentrations. The need for and magnitude of inflammation correction depend on the population group, geographic region, and other factors. Different adjustment methods can lead to variability in the estimated prevalence of iron deficiency. The most suitable adjustment approach should be selected based on the specific country context and used consistently as long as those conditions persist. Both CRP and AGP concentrations may be important to measure, as they reflect different phases of the acute-phase response, ranging from acute infection to chronic inflammation. For example: Reference phase: CRP < 5 mg/L and AGP < 1 g/L. Incubation phase: CRP > 5 mg/L and AGP < 1 g/L. Early convalescence: CRP > 5 mg/L and AGP > 1 g/L. Late convalescence: CRP < 5 mg/L and AGP > 1 g/L. Regression correction methods use linear regression to adjust ferritin concentrations based on CRP and AGP levels and malaria infection status. The adjusted ferritin concentration is calculated as follows: Ferritin (adjusted) = Ferritin (unadjusted) – β1(CRP observed – CRP reference) – β2(AGP observed – AGP reference) – β3(malaria), where β1, β2, and β3 are regression coefficients for CRP, AGP, and malaria, respectively. Due to limited and dispersed data, it is not currently possible to establish population prevalence ranges for defining the magnitude of iron deficiency as a public health problem using ferritin concentrations. However, the prevalence ranges used to determine the severity of anemia as a public health issue may serve as a guide for defining iron deficiency severity based on adjusted ferritin concentrations. Iron interventions in populations with mild, moderate, or severe iron deficiency prevalence could help prevent anemia and mitigate the adverse consequences of iron deficiency, even in the absence of anemia. Research gaps include: Studies comparing ferritin concentrations with bone marrow iron content in healthy, non-infected populations. Validation of methods to adjust iron status indicators for inflammation. Longitudinal studies to assess the role of other iron indicators and their response to interventions. Clarification of ferritin cut-off points in the presence of chronic inflammation or comorbidities like obesity or diabetes. Establishing ferritin cut-off points during pregnancy by trimester. Understanding factors affecting ferritin levels, such as fasting, liver disease, and comorbidities. Utility of ferritin in diagnosing iron overload and establishing cut-off values for all age groups. Comparability of ferritin concentrations across different sample matrices (e.g., venous blood vs. dried serum spots). The WHO will continue monitoring research developments on iron deficiency, particularly regarding biomarkers like ferritin, cut-off values, and the influence of infection/inflammation on iron status diagnosis. If new evidence warrants, the guideline will be updated following WHO's formal procedures.
